# 📊 Sales Data Analysis

What's actually selling, and how does revenue move through the year? This workbook answers that from **real order data** in the sandbox — the `orders` and `products` tables in **Athena** — then teaches the core analyst loop: **query with SQL (DuckDB), then visualize with interactive Plotly**.

**What you'll do**
- Pull real orders joined to their products from Athena into a DataFrame
- Rank products, trend revenue month-over-month, and find each product's best month — all in **SQL cells over the DataFrame**
- Build interactive **Plotly** charts (area, box, scatter) and a static matplotlib trend

All AWS access uses the MicroVM's **execution role** — no credentials in the notebook. Turn on **Reactive** and drag the sliders to re-query live.

```mermaid
graph LR
  O["Athena: orders"] --> J["orders × products (SQL join)"]
  P["Athena: products"] --> J
  J --> R["Rank + trend (SQL over the DataFrame)"]
  R --> V["Interactive Plotly charts"]
  R --> M["matplotlib trend"]
```

## Step 1 · Load real sales — Athena (`orders` × `products`)

The next cell runs one **`read_athena`** query that joins `orders` to `products` so every line carries a real product **name, category, brand, price and cost**. The result is a pandas DataFrame called `sales` that every SQL and chart cell below queries — exactly the analyst pattern of *pull once, slice many ways*.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Real orders joined to products (Athena). One row per order line, with the
# product's category/brand/margin attached — the frame every cell below queries.
sales = read_athena("""
    SELECT o.order_id,
           o.order_date,
           o.quantity,
           o.unit_price,
           o.total                              AS revenue,
           p.product_id,
           p.name                               AS product,
           p.category,
           p.brand,
           ROUND(p.price - p.cost, 2)           AS unit_margin
    FROM microvm_demo_db.orders o
    JOIN microvm_demo_db.products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
""")
# order_date arrives as a real date; make sure it's a datetime for grouping/plots.
sales['date'] = pd.to_datetime(sales['order_date'])
print(f"Loaded {len(sales):,} order lines across {sales['product'].nunique()} products "
      f"and {sales['category'].nunique()} categories")
sales.head(10)

## Step 2 · Rank & trend with SQL (DuckDB)

SQL cells query the `sales` DataFrame directly — DuckDB auto-detects it in the namespace, no upload needed. Three questions a merchandiser always asks: **top sellers**, the **monthly revenue trend** (with a running total), and each product's **best month**.

⚙️ The **Top N** slider feeds the first query via a `{var}` placeholder (`LIMIT {top_n_products}`) — drag it (Reactive on) and the ranked list re-queries.

-- Top products by total revenue (limited by the {top_n_products} scalar param)
SELECT
    product,
    category,
    SUM(quantity)        AS total_units,
    ROUND(SUM(revenue), 2) AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(revenue), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM sales
GROUP BY product, category
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT {top_n_products}

-- Monthly revenue trend with a running (cumulative) total across 2024
SELECT
    strftime(date, '%Y-%m')                              AS month,
    ROUND(SUM(revenue), 2)                               AS monthly_revenue,
    ROUND(SUM(SUM(revenue)) OVER (ORDER BY strftime(date, '%Y-%m')), 2) AS cumulative_revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY strftime(date, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY month

-- Best-selling month per category (which categories peak when?)
SELECT category, best_month, monthly_revenue FROM (
    SELECT category,
           strftime(date, '%Y-%m')                AS best_month,
           ROUND(SUM(revenue), 2)                 AS monthly_revenue,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                              ORDER BY SUM(revenue) DESC) AS rn
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY category, strftime(date, '%Y-%m')
)
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC

## Step 3 · Visualize — interactive Plotly

The payoff: turn the numbers into charts you can zoom, pan, hover, and export. First the **revenue mix by category over the year** (stacked area), then the **spread of order values per category** (box), then **quantity vs revenue** with unit margin as bubble size.

# Interactive: monthly revenue by category (stacked area) — real 2024 seasonality
monthly_cat = (sales.assign(month=sales['date'].dt.to_period('M').dt.to_timestamp())
                    .groupby(['month', 'category'])['revenue'].sum().reset_index())
fig = px.area(
    monthly_cat, x='month', y='revenue', color='category',
    title='Monthly Revenue by Category (2024)',
    labels={'revenue': 'Revenue ($)', 'month': 'Month'},
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2,
)
fig.update_layout(hovermode='x unified')
fig.show()

# Interactive: distribution of order values by category (box plot)
fig = px.box(
    sales, x='category', y='revenue', color='category',
    title='Order-Value Distribution by Category',
    points='outliers',
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Pastel,
)
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, xaxis_title='', yaxis_title='Order value ($)')
fig.show()

# Interactive: quantity vs revenue per order, bubble = unit margin, colored by category
fig = px.scatter(
    sales, x='quantity', y='revenue', color='category', size='unit_margin',
    hover_data=['product', 'date'],
    title='Quantity vs Revenue per order (bubble = unit margin)',
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Bold,
)
fig.show()

## Step 4 · A shareable static chart — matplotlib

Interactive charts are great in the notebook; a static PNG is what you paste into a deck. The same monthly trend rendered with matplotlib.

⚙️ The **Chart width** slider resizes the figure.

# @param {"type": "slider", "min": 6, "max": 16, "step": 2, "default": 10, "label": "Chart width"}
fig_width = 10
# Static matplotlib: total monthly revenue trend across 2024
monthly_revenue = sales.groupby(sales['date'].dt.to_period('M').dt.to_timestamp())['revenue'].sum()
plt.figure(figsize=(fig_width, 5))
plt.plot(monthly_revenue.index, monthly_revenue.values, marker='o', linewidth=2, color='#89b4fa')
plt.fill_between(monthly_revenue.index, monthly_revenue.values, alpha=0.1, color='#89b4fa')
plt.title('Monthly Total Revenue (2024)', color='white', fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel('Month', color='#a6adc8')
plt.ylabel('Revenue ($)', color='#a6adc8')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, color='#a6adc8')
plt.yticks(color='#a6adc8')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

## Step 5 · The helper one-liners — `query_df`, `plot_pie`, `plot_corr`

Steps 3-4 reach for raw `px.*` / matplotlib. The pre-loaded helpers collapse the common cases to a single line (dark theme + column validation + auto-display baked in).

`query_df` runs SQL **across the DataFrames already in memory** — reference each by its variable name, no re-query to Athena. We have three to work with: **`top_products`** (the top sellers from the SQL cell), **`sales`** (every order line), and **`monthly_cat`** (revenue per category per month). The query below **JOINs all three** — enriching each top product with its category's full-year revenue and its single best sales month — exactly the kind of multi-frame stitch that would otherwise be a chain of `pd.merge` + `groupby`. Then `plot_pie` shows revenue share and `plot_corr` surfaces how the numeric fields move together.

# query_df: JOIN THREE in-memory frames by variable name (DuckDB in-process, no AWS
# round-trip) — each top product enriched with its category's full-year revenue and
# its best-selling month. This is the multi-DataFrame stitch query_df is for.
product_brief = query_df('''
    WITH cat_year AS (            -- full-year revenue per category, from every order line
        SELECT category, ROUND(SUM(revenue), 2) AS category_year_revenue
        FROM sales
        GROUP BY category
    ),
    cat_peak AS (                -- each category's single best month, from monthly_cat
        SELECT category, month AS best_month, revenue AS best_month_revenue
        FROM (
            SELECT category, month, revenue,
                   ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn
            FROM monthly_cat
        ) WHERE rn = 1
    )
    SELECT t.product,
           t.category,
           t.total_revenue                       AS product_revenue,
           c.category_year_revenue,
           ROUND(100.0 * t.total_revenue / c.category_year_revenue, 1) AS pct_of_category,
           p.best_month,
           p.best_month_revenue
    FROM top_products t
    JOIN cat_year c  ON t.category = c.category
    JOIN cat_peak  p ON t.category = p.category
    ORDER BY t.total_revenue DESC
''')
product_brief

# plot_pie: revenue share across categories. A quick single-frame query_df feeds it.
cat_rev = query_df('''
    SELECT category, ROUND(SUM(revenue), 2) AS revenue
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY category
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
''')
plot_pie(cat_rev, names='category', values='revenue', title='Revenue Share by Category')

# plot_corr: correlation heatmap of the numeric order fields — the EDA companion to
# profile(). Auto-selects numeric columns (needs ≥2); here: quantity, unit_price,
# revenue, unit_margin.
plot_corr(sales, title='Order Metrics — Correlation')
